newsitem.title: FRANCE: FIGURE SKATING-CANDELORO READY TO SKATE IN PAIN.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-CANDELORO READY TO SKATE IN PAIN.

text.p: If Philippe Candeloro succeeds in beating his rivals from the former Soviet Union this week, he will do it skating in pain.
The popular Frenchman still aches on landing some jumps despite surgery last May on an ankle injury that affected him last season.
But he is still western Europe's best hope at the European championships against the might of three men from Russia, three from Ukraine and a former Russian now skating for Azerbaijan.
The Russians include Olympic champion Alexei Urmanov, ex-European champion Ilya Kulik and impressive 16-year-old Alexei Yagudin.
Ukraine's trio comprises holder Viacheslav Zagorodniuk, former champion Dmitry Dmitrenko and the surprise winner of one of the two qualifying groups on Sunday, Evgeny Pliuta.
The Azerbaijani is Igor Pashkevitch, who became disenchanted at finishing second for Russia a year ago only to be dropped for the subsequent world championships in place of Urmanov.
Candeloro seems to be itching for battle despite the loss of training time towards the end of last year while the injury on his right ankle healed enough for him to resume training.
"It has been a short season because I started only in November," said Candeloro, a former silver medallist in both the European and world championships.
"It hasn't been easy but we found something that works for me in training, and it is much better now.
"But there is still pain landing the flip and the lutz. I expect to feel pain all season and you never know how much it is going to hurt.
"I really should have had a full year to recover," he said.

Candeloro needed the operation because a piece of bone in his right ankle was affecting a ligament and led to his disappointing fifth and ninth place finishes in last year's two international championships.
But he has buckled down seriously since November when he went to the NHK Trophy in Tokyo and finished seventh in a strong field in the Champions Series event after only two weeks of preparation.
"I skated well there, again," he said, referring to his silver medal in the 1994 world championships there.
That second place came a month after he took bronze at the 1994 Olympics in Lillehammer, and now he is aiming at next year's Olympics in Nagano, Japan.
"That was why I skated at the NHK. "It was important for me to keep the feeling with the Japanese fans," he said.
The injury has, however, delayed his development of a quadruple jump, which he feels will be essential at Nagano.
"You've seen the skaters trying it this week because they will need it for the Olympic Games. But I have not been able to work on it.
"Perhaps I will between this event and the world championships - if there is no risk," he said.
His first aim this week will be to come successfully through the short programme on Wednesday, when missed elements can ruin all hopes of a medal.
"I have to be third or fourth so I can be in the last group in the free skating on Thursday," he said.
"Last year I skated so bad in the short programme that I was too far back for the free skating. Nobody cares what you do when you're 10th or worse in the short."
